Intelligence + memory
The difference between a tool and someone who knows the account .
The client who will not run video. The market that looks unprofitable and is not. The suggestion you have now rejected four times. None of it is in the ad platforms — it is why a new hire takes a quarter to become useful, and why generic AI still sounds like a stranger on day ninety.
Learned, not configured. No setup screen to abandon half-filled. It picks rules up as you say them, shows you what it heard, and holds it only once you confirm.
Week eight reads differently from week one. The rejected suggestion stops arriving. The number you actually judge on becomes the default. The brief gets shorter because what it knows is no longer re-argued.
Yours, and cross-platform. Your rules follow the brand across every platform you connect — and a limit set in July still stops a change proposed in September.

The blind spot
The platform can't see the number that decides it.
An ad platform optimizes toward what its pixel can measure. It never sees your cost of goods, your margin, or what a customer is worth on the second order. So when it finds a campaign that converts cheaply and loses money on every order, it does the logical thing: it scales it. Nobody is asleep at the wheel — the dashboard is green, the target is met, and the report is correct on its own terms. That is the expensive part.
it wakes up
Platform lens
What the pixel measures
ROAS 3.2× healthy
Conversions are up and return on ad spend is above target.
Verdict: scale it
the revenue line
Ground truth
What your business knows
Margin negative on this cohort
The volume is discount-driven. Thin contribution per order, and these buyers rarely come back.
Verdict: stop
Same campaign. Two verdicts. Only one of them is looking at your profit — and it isn't the one spending your budget.
Reconciled against your own revenue
Adgent reads GA4 and Search Console alongside the ad platforms, so a report is checked against a source the platform does not control. Shopify reading is the next connection we are building — that is what closes the loop to money that actually landed.
A structural gap, not a feature gap
No optimizer built inside an ad platform can grade its own spend against your margin. It doesn't have the data, and it isn't neutral about the answer.
Judgment, not just another chart
An audit tells you what happened. Adgent takes the position — what to do about it — and remembers the calls you've already made on this brand.
it seals
Trust Gate · one real account, two refusals
It said no. Twice. Before a dollar was spent.
"This pixel can't teach a campaign yet"
Thirty days: 65,042 custom events, 16,404 initiate-checkout — and 4 purchases. Meta's own docs put the floor at 50 events in 7 days [developers.meta.com]. Technically possible to build. Nothing there for the optimiser to learn from.
"Your target is unreachable — here's why"
Asked for a ₺250 cost per conversion. The account's own history at the booking stage sits near ₺4,000 . At 250 the only reachable thing is a ₺13 micro-lead that clears the target and books nobody.
Trust Gate
The test of a thinking tool: does it ever tell you no ?
Anything that only says yes is executing, not reasoning. Both refusals came from one real account, unprompted, before any budget moved — each showing the account's own numbers as the reason. A tool that checks this afterwards reports the same facts a month later, once the money has already taught the algorithm nothing.
Creative intelligence
It reads every creative like a strategist — not a tagger.
Creative is the single biggest driver of a campaign's sales — 49% , more than targeting (11%) or reach (14%) [NCSolutions / Circana, 2023]. It is also the layer most tools only tag. Adgent reads every live ad the way a senior buyer would — its DNA, the story scene by scene, and exactly where viewers leave. No upload step: it reads what is already running.
it reads

Creative DNA
Every ad, decoded: hook, format, persona, angle, offer, visuals and audio — so you can see why a creative works, not just that it did.
Scene-by-scene storyboard
Video ads broken down shot by shot — what happens in each moment, so a weak opening or a slow middle is obvious at a glance.
Where viewers leave
A creative funnel that tracks the hold-curve across your ads — the exact scene where attention drops, so you fix the leak instead of guessing.
Fatigue, verdict-first
It flags the creatives wearing out — before the numbers slide — and hands you a dollar-valued refresh you can apply from chat.
Why Adgent
Analyze or act — everything else makes you choose.
Reporting tools go deep but never touch the account. Platform AIs act, but with no judgment and never on your side. Adgent does both — and remembers your brand. Seven layers sit between a connected ad account and a decision you would stand behind; most tools stop at the audit.

Questions
Good questions, answered plainly.
it answers
Does Adgent change my campaigns on its own?
No. Access is read-only by default. When a fix or a campaign is ready, Adgent prepares it and waits — you apply it from chat with one message. The control is always yours; nothing is automatic.
Which ad platforms does it cover?
Meta and Google Ads, read and reasoned about as one account — and it pulls in GA4 and Search Console so reports are checked against a source the platform does not control. Shopify is the next connection we are building.
What can I actually do from chat?
Ask about any ad, campaign, or account; run placement and demographic audits; generate custom reports; apply prepared fixes; and build cross-channel campaigns — all by message.
What is the Trust Gate?
It's how Adgent stays honest about numbers. If a campaign optimizes toward a value-less event, or a metric is still inside Meta's 7-day attribution window, we flag it rather than report a confident figure. We'd rather tell you a number can't be trusted than pretend it can.
How do I know an agent won't spam me?
Two things stop it. First, the agent has a quiet mechanism built into it, not bolted on: a condition has to hold for several evaluations before it fires, there is a cooldown after it does, and the metric has to recover before the same alert can come back — so something sitting on the threshold does not alert you twice an hour. Second, you can preview a threshold agent against your own account history before you publish it: how often it would have fired, and on what. Adjust the threshold and the answer updates, all before anything reaches you.
Will it really pay for itself?
In our audits, a single account's first pass typically surfaces meaningful recoverable spend — before counting the hours it saves your team. Talk to sales and we'll show you what Adgent finds in your account.
Who is Adgent for?
Agencies managing many accounts, ecommerce brands running their own spend, in-house growth teams, and independent performance marketers — anyone who'd rather talk to an analyst than decode a dashboard.
Still deciding?

# Adgent features — what an AI media buyer actually does
URL: https://adgent.app/features

id="main" tabindex="-1">
Features
Eight things a senior buyer does. Every morning.
Not a feature list — a job description.
Each of these is a piece of work someone on your team is doing by hand right now,
or not doing at all because there are more accounts than there are hours.
Eight jobs, one loop, ending where you approve it.
01
Daily verdict
Every account read overnight — the position first, the evidence under it
You do not open a dashboard and start hunting. Adgent reads every connected account while you sleep, ranks what it found by what it costs you, and writes the verdict in plain language. The account that needs you today is at the top; the ones that are fine say so in one line.
A morning brief ranked by impact, not by alphabet
One health score per account, so a book of twenty is scannable
Anomalies caught against the account's own history, not a generic threshold
See how it works
02
Ground truth
Judged on the number that decides it, not the number the pixel can see
An ad platform optimizes toward what its own pixel measures. It never sees your cost of goods, your return rate, or what a customer is worth on the second order. So when a campaign converts cheaply and loses money on every order, it does the logical thing and scales it. Adgent reads GA4 and Search Console alongside the ad platforms today, and Shopify is the next connection we are building — the one that closes the loop to money that actually landed.
Reconciled against your own revenue, not platform-reported conversions
A structural gap, not a feature gap — no in-platform optimizer can grade its own spend against your margin
The position stated, with the money attached to it
See how it works
03
Trust Gate
The test of a thinking tool: does it ever tell you no?
Anything that only says yes is executing, not reasoning. When a pixel has too little signal to teach a campaign, or a target is unreachable given the account's own history, Adgent refuses and shows you the numbers behind the refusal — before any budget moves, not in a report a month later.
Refuses unreachable targets, with the account's own history as the reason
Flags metrics still inside an attribution window instead of reporting a confident figure
Catches campaigns optimizing toward an event that carries no value
See how it works
04
Creative intelligence
It reads every creative like a strategist — not a tagger
Creative is the single biggest driver of a campaign's sales. It is also the layer most tools only tag. Adgent reads every live ad the way a senior buyer would: its DNA, the story scene by scene, and exactly where viewers leave. No upload step — it reads what is already running.
Scene-by-scene decomposition joined to per-moment retention
The hold curve: where viewers leave, and what was on screen when they did
Fatigue flagged before the numbers slide, with a valued refresh you can apply from chat
See how it works
05
Change Ledger
Every change logged with what it replaced — and undoable on your approval
Every change Adgent makes is written to a ledger with the state it replaced, labelled reversible or not before you approve it, and put back on your approval. Platform-side changes are read from Meta and Google's own change feeds and surfaced in your Overview, so a drift you did not cause still has a date and an actor. The ledger also does a second job nobody asks of it: a change you can undo and redo is a change you can settle, instead of argue about.
Before-state captured on every write, with actor and source attribution
Reversible or not — labelled before you approve, not discovered after
Adgent's own writes are reversible; platform-side changes are read and surfaced
See how it works
06
Account memory
You explain the account once
Your rules, your exceptions, the calls you have already made — Adgent picks them up from the way you work and carries them into every verdict after. Nothing to configure, and nothing to repeat next month. A generic tool restarts from zero every session; here the context accumulates, and it is yours.
Learned from how you talk to it, not from a setup screen
Shown to you and confirmed before it is remembered — and overridable
Follows the brand across every platform you connect, not locked to one
See how it works
07
Dashboards & standing reports
Describe the view. It gets built, and it stays live.
The cut you want — the platforms, the window, the breakdown, the metric you judge on — described in one message and built on your data rather than configured in a form. What comes back stays wired to the account, so sharing it with a client does not turn it into a screenshot that is wrong by Thursday. Make it standing and it rebuilds itself before the Monday call, or watches one metric and stays quiet until that metric moves.
Custom reports generated from a single message
Live dashboards you can share read-only, not static exports
Standing agents that report only when the thing they watch changes
See how it works
08
Media planning
A plan where every number shows where it came from
The plan arrives as data, not a deck: budget split by platform, flight dates, line items with their buying types, and a cost range on each one — with the source campaigns and the window printed underneath every range. Where the account has no history for a market, it produces no estimate at all and recommends a short test instead. It lands as a Draft; nothing is applied until you approve it.
Every cost range names the campaigns and window it was read from
No history means no number — a test window instead of a plausible guess
Assumptions, measurement caveats and open questions carried in the plan itself
See how it works
09
Campaign builds
Drafted whole from a description — and held, paused, for you
Structure, budget, targeting, copy and the creative slots, prefilled from what this account has actually proven rather than from a template — with the reason printed beside each choice, including the ones it declined. It blocks in the form where you can still fix things: a missing creative stops the build there, not after approval. What you approve is created paused, so switching it on is a second, separate decision.
Every field prefilled from this account's own history, with the evidence named
Refuses the build when the conversion signal cannot support it — before you spend
Created paused, logged in the ledger, reversible like every other write
See how it works
By team

Underneath all eight
None of it works without the layers under it.
A verdict needs memory, memory needs correct data, and execution needs all of it. That order is the product — and it is why the list above cannot be assembled from parts.
Worth pricing what the next quarter of not deciding costs. Eight jobs, done by hand or not at all, for another ninety mornings: that is roughly ninety un-read accounts per account you own, every creative graded on two scalars, and every platform-side setting change discovered whenever someone happens to look. None of it shows up as a line item. It shows up as the campaign you scaled in March and stopped in June.

# Why Adgent — analyze or act, everything else makes you choose
URL: https://adgent.app/why-adgent

id="main" tabindex="-1">
Why Adgent
Analyze or act. Everything else makes you choose.
The tools that understand your account can't touch it. The ones that touch it don't understand it.
That split is not an accident of the market — it is what happens when analysis and execution
are built by different kinds of company, for different reasons. Adgent was built as one thing.
This page is the argument, and then the architecture underneath it.
Each row is buyable somewhere. The column is not.
The four options on the table
Every one of them is a reasonable purchase.
This is not a page about bad products. Each category below does its job well, and most teams own two or three of them already. The question is what happens in the gap between them — because that gap is where the money leaks.
Category Reporting & BI tools
What they're genuinely good at: pulling every platform into one place, joining it to your store and your CRM, and rendering it faster and prettier than a native dashboard ever will.
Where it stops: a chart is a description of the past. It has no opinion, so the work of turning it into a decision is still yours — and that work is the expensive part, done by your most expensive person, every morning.
The tell: you have the dashboard, and you still don't know what to do on Monday.
Category The ad platform's own AI
What it's genuinely good at: it sees the auction from the inside, in real time, at a resolution no third party gets. For finding volume inside its own inventory, nothing beats it.
Where it stops: it optimizes toward what its own pixel can measure, and it is not neutral about the answer. It cannot see your cost of goods or what a customer is worth on the second order — so a campaign that converts cheaply and loses money on every order gets scaled, correctly, by its own logic.
The tell: the dashboard is green and the P&L disagrees.
Category Rule-based automation
What it's genuinely good at: doing the boring thing at 3am without being asked. A well-written rule is fast, cheap and completely predictable.
Where it stops: a rule fires on a threshold, not on a reason. It cannot tell a creative that is wearing out from a week that was seasonally soft, and it will happily pause the wrong thing at speed. Rules also rot: nobody remembers why the 2024 one exists, so nobody deletes it.
The tell: a folder of rules, and no one willing to touch them.
Category Another pair of human hands
What it's genuinely good at: judgment, context, and accountability. A good senior buyer is still the best thing that can happen to an account, and this page is not an argument against hiring one.
Where it stops: it does not scale, it costs the most, and it is the layer under the most pressure — the accounts per person keep climbing. The junior work of reading every account every morning is exactly the work seniors stop doing first.
The tell: the account nobody opened this week is the one you worry about.
Notice the pattern: the two categories with judgment can't act at scale, and the two that act at scale have no judgment. That is the gap.
Owning two or three of these and deciding later is itself a decision, and it has a price. Another quarter in the gap is another quarter of the dashboard being right and Monday still being unclear, of the platform scaling toward its own pixel, of rules nobody will touch, and of the account nobody opened. Doing nothing feels free because none of that arrives as an invoice — it arrives as the spend you would not have approved if someone had read it in time.
The same four, row by row
Where each one stops .
The categories above, scored on the things a buyer actually has to have. Every row is available somewhere — the question is whether you can get them from one place, in an order that holds.
Capability
Reporting tools
Platform AIs
Automation rules
Adgent
Executes across platforms — ✓ ✓ ✓
Reasons about account structure — — — ✓
Deep config & measurement diagnostics ✓ — — ✓
Chat-native verdicts + live reports — — — ✓
Remembers your brand's rules — — — ✓
One column checked all the way down. That column is the whole point.
Each row on its own is buyable somewhere. The reason no column but ours is checked all the way down is that the top rows only work if the ones under them do — judgment needs memory, and memory needs a year of your history in one place. That order is the product.
How we're built
Touching the platform is easy. Knowing what to do is hard.
Seven layers sit between a connected ad account and a decision you'd stand behind. Most tools stop at the audit. Everything above it is the hard part.
it stacks
L6 · Operating surface The morning brief, a queue of things worth acting on, chat, live dashboards, and a workspace that lists every account you run with its own score, so you can see which to open first.
A chat window wired to some data sources is not a product. The daily surface your team actually works in is.
L5 · Safe execution Read-only until you say otherwise. Every write is logged with its before-state, labelled reversible or not before you approve, and undone on your approval. Each company's data sits in its own database file.
Pointing a model at a live ad account is the easy part and the dangerous part. The ledger also does a second job nobody asks of it: a change you can undo and redo is a change you can settle, instead of argue about.
L4 · Judgment Root cause rather than symptom, compared fairly across platforms, with the decision stated and the money attached to it.
The audit plus memory is what makes a position possible: not "here's what moved," but "here's what to do, and here's what it's worth."
L3 · Memory Context that survives the session: what was looked at, what was decided, and what you've told it about how this brand runs.
Memory is what turns an audit into judgment. A generic tool restarts from zero every time; here the context accumulates, across platforms, and it's yours.
L2 · Audit What happened and where — trends, anomalies against the account's own history and its peers, breakdowns by placement, device and geography. Then the same audit on the creative: its DNA, the story scene by scene, and where viewers drop off.
Everyone can get you to the account numbers. Reading the creative this way is rarer — but it still only tells you what happened. Nobody takes the next step for you.
L1 · Data correctness A year of history, synced daily, with attribution normalized and conversion events reconciled into one comparable shape across platforms.
Raw platform output is not decision-ready. Skip this and you get answers delivered with total confidence and no basis — the most expensive kind of wrong.
L0 · Connectivity Reads your accounts directly from the ad platforms, and pulls in analytics and store data alongside them.
This layer only answers "can it reach the account." It's getting cheaper for everyone — which helps us, because it isn't what we sell.
L6 Operating surface Your daily surface
L5 Safe execution The trust layer
L4 Judgment The decision
L3 Memory Audit → judgment
where most tools stop
L2 Audit What happened, and where
L1 Data correctness No confident-but-wrong
L0 Connectivity Reads your accounts
The audit is the ceiling of the category. Memory, judgment and safe execution are the three layers above it — and they're where the work of the last year went.
Why the order matters
You cannot buy layer four without the three under it.
This is not a feature list where you pick the rows you like. Each layer is load-bearing for the one above it, which is why a tool that starts at the top produces confident answers with nothing underneath them.
Judgment needs memory
A verdict is a position, and a position depends on what you already decided. Without memory, every session restarts from zero and the tool re-suggests the thing you rejected last month — which is how people stop reading the output.
Memory needs correct data
Remembering a wrong number is worse than not remembering. Attribution windows differ per platform, conversion events are named inconsistently, and a naive join across Meta and Google produces a comparison that looks clean and is not.
Execution needs all of it
Writing to a live ad account is easy to build and expensive to get wrong. A write is only safe when the system knows what the number means, what you already decided, and how to put it back.
The uncomfortable version: most of the category is a very good layer two. That is a real product and it sells. It just is not a decision.
The trust layer, in detail
Three locks, and a change has to pass all three .
Layer five is the one people ask about first, so here it is in full. None of these is a setting you have to find and switch on.
01
Read-only until you say otherwise
A connected account starts with no write access at all. Adgent analyses, ranks and proposes — and cannot touch the account until execution is explicitly turned on for it.
02
Nothing applies without approval
Every proposed change is shown with its before-state, what it costs, and whether it can be undone — labelled before you approve, not discovered after. You approve from the same chat where you found it.
03
Reversible, on your approval
Every change Adgent makes is written to a ledger with the state it replaced, and put back from the same chat. Platform-side changes are read and surfaced separately, so drift you did not cause still carries a date and an actor. A change you can undo is a change you can settle rather than argue about.
And underneath all three: physical isolation
Each company's analytical data lives in its own database file, not a shared table with a customer column in it. The separation is structural, so a query cannot reach across it even by mistake.
Security in detail &rarr; What we do with your data &rarr; Inside the Change Ledger &rarr;
The honest version
What we would tell you not to buy us for.
A comparison page where the vendor wins every row is not a comparison, it is a brochure. Here is where the other options are the right call.
If you need creative generated
Adgent reads creative, it does not make it. Its analysis is deliberately scoped to what is already running — DNA, story beat by beat, and where viewers leave. If you want ads produced, that is a different tool and we will say so.
If you want it to run unattended
There is no mode where Adgent spends without a human approving. If what you want is hands-off autonomous buying, we are the wrong shape — and that is a design decision, not a missing feature.
If one small account is all you run
Below a certain spend, the daily read is a luxury and the platform's own tools plus an hour a week will get you most of the way. The value here scales with how many accounts go un-read.
The three questions people actually ask
The objections, answered before you have to raise them.
&ldquo;What stops it doing something stupid with my budget?&rdquo;
Three things, in order: it starts read-only and cannot write until you turn execution on; nothing applies until you approve it, with the before-state and the cost shown; and every applied change is logged with what it replaced, undoable on your approval. It also refuses — an unreachable target gets pushed back on, with the account's own history as the reason, before any money moves.
See the Trust Gate &rarr; See the Change Ledger &rarr;
&ldquo;How is this different from asking a general AI assistant?&rdquo;
A general model with your data pasted in has no memory of your account, no reconciled history to reason over, and no way to act. The layers underneath are the difference: a year of history normalized into one comparable shape, memory of the calls you already made, and a write path that logs and reverses. Without those, you get fluent answers with nothing behind them.
See the seven layers &rarr;
&ldquo;We already have a dashboard. Why add another tool?&rdquo;
You are not short on data — you are short on someone reading it in time. The dashboard tells you what happened; it does not tell you which of your accounts needs you this morning, or take a position on what to do about it. If your dashboard is already being read every day by someone senior, you may not need us. Most teams are honest that it isn't.
See the daily verdict &rarr;
Judge it against what you already own
Give it one account for one week, beside the tools you already pay for.
The argument on this page is only worth as much as it survives on your own account. Pick one, run the read next to your dashboard and your platform's recommendations for a week, and settle it on your own numbers rather than ours.

# The daily verdict on every ad account — Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/daily-verdict

id="main" tabindex="-1">
Daily verdict
Every account read before you open your laptop.
You should not have to go hunting for the problem. Adgent reads every connected account overnight, ranks what it found by what it is costing you, and writes the answer in plain language. The account that needs you today is at the top. The ones that are fine say so in one line and get out of your way.
The brief, ranked by what it costs you
The shape of it
A verdict is a position , not a summary.
Most morning emails are a list of numbers that went up and down. That is a description of yesterday, and it leaves the actual work — deciding what it means — exactly where it was.
What a report gives you
CPA up 18% week on week
Spend flat, impressions down 9%
Campaign 4 above target, Campaign 7 below
Frequency 3.4, up from 2.9
All true. All still your problem to interpret, at 8:40am, on every account you run.
What a verdict gives you
Campaign 7 is the one to touch today. Its CPA rise is not seasonal — the top creative crossed frequency 3.4 and hold rate fell with it.
Campaign 4 needs nothing. The dip is a two-day weekend pattern this account shows every month.
The fix is a creative refresh, not a bid change. Bidding down here buys cheaper impressions of an ad people have stopped watching.
The evidence sits underneath every line. You can disagree with it — but you are disagreeing with a position, not staring at a chart.
In the morning brief
What is the verdict on Northlight this morning?
Prospecting CPA is up 34% week on week, and it is not seasonal. The top creative crossed frequency 3.4 on Tuesday and hold rate fell with it — that pairing is what makes it fatigue rather than an auction shift. This is Northlight&rsquo;s own read. I do not compare it against your other accounts — each one is analysed inside itself.
Why not just bid down?
Because the auction is not the problem. Bidding down here buys cheaper impressions of an ad people have stopped watching — you would pay less per view and lose the same money more slowly. The fix is a creative refresh , and I have costed it: roughly £2,400 of recoverable spend over the next fortnight.
Northlight &#183; this morning one account
One account, read on its own. The findings inside it are ranked by recoverable spend.
What makes the ranking honest
Ranked by what it costs , not by what changed most.
A 60% swing on a campaign spending forty dollars a day is noise wearing a big percentage. Sorting by volatility puts noise at the top of your morning; sorting by money puts the decision there.
Against its own history
An anomaly is measured against how this account normally behaves — its own weekday shape, its own seasonality — not a generic threshold that fires every Monday and gets ignored by Wednesday.
Against its peers
The same ad set is also compared with the others in its account. A campaign can be down and still be the healthiest thing you own, which changes what you should do about it.
Against your real revenue
Platform-reported conversions are the starting point, not the answer. The verdict reconciles them against what actually landed, so a campaign that looks efficient and loses money does not get promoted to the top as a success.
One health score per account
A book of twenty accounts, scannable in a minute .
The hard part of running many accounts is not analysing one of them. It is knowing which one to analyse. Each account is read on its own and carries a single score with the reason attached; the workspace sorts those scores so triage takes a glance rather than twenty logins. It is an ordering of separate reads — the analysis itself never leaves the account it is in.
Including the account you cannot afford to lose, on the week it looked fine
Every team already puts someone on the accounts that are visibly struggling. The expensive one is the retainer that has been quiet for six weeks — no fire, no complaint, nothing to escalate — so it gets a glance instead of a read, and the leak runs until the renewal conversation. That account gets the same overnight read as the one on fire, and if the read finds nothing it says so in one line.
How this works across a book of clients &rarr;

Two things decide whether a morning read is worth reading: whether it is measured against money that actually landed, and whether it is willing to tell you something you do not want to hear.

# Ground truth — judged on your margin — Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/ground-truth

id="main" tabindex="-1">
Ground truth
The platform can't see the number that decides it.
An ad platform optimises toward what its own pixel can measure. It never sees your cost of goods, your return rate, or what a customer is worth on the second order. So when it finds a campaign that converts cheaply and loses money on every order, it does the logical thing: it scales it. Nobody is asleep at the wheel — the dashboard is green, the target is met, and the report is correct on its own terms. That is the expensive part.
Same campaign. Two verdicts. One is looking at profit.
Platform lens
What the pixel measures
ROAS 3.2× healthy
Conversions are up and return on ad spend is above target.
Verdict: scale it
the revenue line
Ground truth
What your business knows
Margin negative on this cohort
The volume is discount-driven. Thin contribution per order, and these buyers rarely come back.
Verdict: stop
Same campaign. Two verdicts. Only one of them is looking at your profit — and it isn't the one spending your budget.
Asking about a campaign that looks fine
Scale campaign 12? It is our best ROAS this month.
I would not. Platform ROAS is 3.2×, which is genuinely your best. But the orders behind it carry a 41% average discount and an 8% return rate — the contribution on that cohort is negative. It is your best campaign at acquiring volume and your worst at acquiring profit. The platform can only see the first half.
Where are you getting the discount rate?
From your analytics, not from Meta — I reconcile platform-reported conversions against what actually landed. Store reading (orders, cost per item, refunds) is the next connection we are building; today this comes from GA4.
Reconciled view Campaign 12
The disagreement is the finding, not an error.
Why this is not fixable inside the platform
It is a structural gap, not a feature gap.
This is worth being precise about, because it is the difference between a thing that gets patched in the next release and a thing that cannot be patched at all.
It does not have the data
Your cost of goods lives in your store or your ERP. Your return rate shows up weeks after the click. Your second-order value lives in a cohort nobody has sent to the ad platform, and mostly should not.
It is not neutral about the answer
An optimiser grading its own spend is being asked to mark its own homework. Even a perfectly honest one is measuring the objective it was given, and that objective is volume of a measurable event — not profit.
The report is correct and the conclusion is wrong
This is what makes it expensive. Nothing looks broken. There is no error state, no alert, no red number — just a well-run campaign steadily scaling something that loses money per order.
Which is why waiting a quarter is not neutral. Nothing in the account will surface this on its own — the 3.2× campaign above keeps clearing its target, keeps earning budget, and keeps teaching the optimiser that discount-driven volume is what you want more of. Ninety days of that is not ninety days of no decision. It is ninety days of one decision, made by the system with the least visibility into your profit.
What Adgent reads instead
Reconciled against the numbers your business runs on.
Adgent reads GA4 and Search Console alongside the ad platforms, so a report is checked against a source the platform does not control — and where the two disagree, the disagreement itself is the finding. Shopify reading is the next connection we are building.
Connected today
Meta Ads connected
Google Ads connected
GA4 connected
Search Console connected
Merchant Center connected
Next
Shopify next
Salesforce & HubSpot next
TikTok Ads later
Reads are read-only. A connector is listed here only once it is running in the product — the ones marked next are being built, and we would rather show you the line than blur it.
01
Store revenue, not platform-reported revenue
Platform-attributed conversions and what your store recorded are two different numbers, and the gap between them is usually the whole argument. Both are shown, with the gap named.
02
Attribution normalised across platforms
Meta and Google count a conversion over different windows with different rules. Comparing them raw produces a clean-looking chart that is not a comparison. Adgent puts them into one comparable shape first.
03
The verdict follows the money
Once the numbers reconcile, the position changes. "Scale this" and "stop this" can be the correct call on the same campaign depending on which lens you are looking through — and only one of those lenses is looking at your profit.
Where this bites hardest
Discount-driven volume is the classic case: cheap conversions, thin contribution per order, buyers who rarely come back. Every measurable signal says winner. The only lens that disagrees is the one the platform does not have.
Next
Ground truth is what makes a verdict worth reading.
Reconciled numbers are the input; a position you can act on is the output. And the reason no in-platform tool closes this gap is the same reason the comparison page exists.

# The Trust Gate — a tool that can say no — Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/trust-gate

id="main" tabindex="-1">
Trust Gate
The test of a thinking tool: does it ever tell you no ?
Anything that only says yes is executing, not reasoning. A tool that accepts every target you type and every campaign you ask for is not being helpful — it is being agreeable, which is the cheapest thing software can be. The Trust Gate is the part of Adgent that pushes back, with the account's own numbers as the reason, before any budget moves.
A real refusal, from a real account
Asking for something the account cannot do
Set the target to ₺250 cost per conversion.
I can, but I would be setting you up. This account has never come near that at the booking stage — its own history sits around ₺4,000. At ₺250 the only reachable conversion is a ₺13 micro-lead that clears the target and books nobody. You would hit the number and lose the quarter.
What is actually achievable?
On the last ninety days, ₺2,800&ndash;3,400 is defensible, and there is a real path to the low ₺2,000s if we fix the event definition first — three of your five conversion actions currently carry no value at all. Want me to show which?
Where the target lands on this account
₺250 is not a stretch. It is a different event .
Between the ask and the outcome sits a second problem: thirty days of this pixel hold 65,042 custom events, 16,404 initiate-checkouts and 4 purchases — against Meta&rsquo;s own floor of 50 events in 7 days . [developers.meta.com]
Both refusals came from one real account, unprompted, before a dollar was spent. A tool that checks this afterwards reports the same facts a month later — once the money has already taught the algorithm nothing.
That account is still running. Left alone another quarter, the pixel with 4 purchases in thirty days keeps training on nothing, and the ₺250 target keeps getting hit by the ₺13 micro-lead that books nobody — so the number on the report improves while the bookings do not. Nothing here fails loudly enough to interrupt anyone. That is the whole reason it survives a quarter.
What it refuses
Three kinds of no, and why each one saves money.
01
"This pixel can't teach a campaign yet"
Below a certain volume of the right event, an optimiser has nothing to learn from. Launching anyway is technically possible and produces a campaign that spends while learning nothing. Adgent says so before the launch, not in the post-mortem.
02
"Your target is unreachable — here's why"
Ask for a cost per conversion far below anything the account has ever achieved and something has to give. Usually what gives is the definition of the conversion: the target gets hit by a micro-event that converts nobody. The refusal shows the account's own history as the reason.
03
"This number isn't ready to be trusted"
A metric still inside its attribution window will move on its own. Reporting it as final produces confident figures that quietly revise themselves later. Adgent flags it instead of giving you a number that will change.
Why this matters more with AI, not less
Confident nonsense is the failure. Refusal is the pass .
The characteristic failure of a language model pointed at a data set is fluency without grounds — an answer that reads beautifully and is not supported by anything. In a reporting tool that costs you an afternoon. Wired to a live ad account, it costs you budget.
It refuses before spending, not after
Timing is the whole value. An audit that finds the same problem four weeks later is describing money that is already gone.
It shows the numbers behind the no
A refusal without evidence is just an obstacle, and people route around obstacles. Every refusal carries the account's own figures, so you can overrule it on purpose rather than out of frustration.
You can still say do it anyway
This is a gate, not a lock. Sometimes you know something the data does not — a launch, a promotion, a client's decision. The point is that you make that call knowingly.
Next
Refusing is one half. Being able to undo is the other.
The Trust Gate stops the change that should not happen. The Change Ledger handles the one that should not have happened — and both sit on the same execution layer.
Change Ledger
Every change logged with the state it replaced, and undone on your approval.
Read more
The seven layers
What sits between a connected account and a decision.
Read more
Ask it something it should refuse
Try to make it tell you what you want to hear.
Bring a target you suspect is unreachable, or a campaign you think is optimising toward nothing. The interesting outcome is the one where it pushes back.
Refusals come with the account's own history attached
Before the budget moves, not in the post-mortem
You can still overrule it — knowingly
What comes back
Every target and event it would question on your account today, with the numbers behind each objection. Including the ones you will disagree with.

# Creative intelligence, scene by scene — Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/creative-intelligence

id="main" tabindex="-1">
Creative intelligence
It reads every creative like a strategist — not a tagger.
Creative is the single biggest driver of a campaign's sales — 49%, more than targeting (11%) or reach (14%) [NCSolutions / Circana, 2023]. It is also the layer most tools only tag. Adgent reads every live ad the way a senior buyer would: its DNA, the story scene by scene, and exactly where viewers leave. No upload step — it reads what is already running.
The hold curve, read against the storyboard — one scene explains the loss
The difference that matters
A tag says what is in the ad. A read says what the ad does .
Most creative analytics stops at attributes: this ad has a person, a kitchen, a price overlay, a voiceover. That is a filing system. It tells you what you already knew when you briefed it.
Tagging
Has: product close-up, female presenter, text overlay
Format: 9:16 video, 14 seconds
Hook rate 31%, hold rate 12%
Two scalars and a list of nouns. Nothing here tells you which second to change.
Reading it
Retention holds through the demo and collapses at 0:07 — the second the price overlay lands, before the benefit is stated.
The hook is doing its job. Losing viewers at seven seconds is not a thumbnail problem, and changing the opening frame would fix nothing.
The fix is order, not content. The same three scenes, with the price after the payoff instead of before it.
Same ad, same data. One of these is a decision you can hand to an editor.
Creatives &#8250; SPRING_LAUNCH_V3
Spend &#183; 28d &#163;41,280
Impressions 2.4M
CTR 1.12% &#8722;0.3pt
Hook rate 71% +4pt
ROAS &#183; purchase 2.1× was 3.4×
Creative DNA VLM &#183; AUTO
FORMAT Talking head
HOOK Question
SETTING Kitchen
PROOF Price overlay
Dossier VLM READING
Presenter states the problem, demonstrates, then the offer. On-screen text carries the price before the benefit lands.
Where viewers leave RETENTION × STORYBOARD
0:00
0:03
0:07
0:11
0:00 Hook &#183; question to camera &#8722;9% viewers
0:03 Demonstration &#8722;12% viewers
0:07 Price overlay &#8722;38% viewers &#183; biggest drop
0:11 Offer and end card &#8722;6% viewers
Diagnosis CTR × CVR DECISION TREE
Creative fatigue — hook wear-out
Three reads on every live ad
DNA, the story, and where they leave .
Two ads can share a format, a length and a hook rate and still be built from different arguments. The DNA is the part that makes them comparable — what the ad promises, how it proves it, and in what order — so a winner can be repeated on purpose instead of guessed at.
01
Creative DNA
What the ad is actually built from — its structural pattern, its promise, the shape of its argument. This is what lets one account's winners be compared with each other rather than ranked by spend.
02
The storyboard, scene by scene
The ad decomposed into its beats, in order, with what each one is doing. A fifteen-second video is not one thing; it is five decisions, and usually only one of them is wrong.
03
The hold curve
Where viewers leave, joined to what was on screen when they did. This is the join that matters: a retention chart without the scene under it tells you people left, not why.
Fatigue, flagged before the numbers slide
A creative wearing out shows up in the read before it shows up in the CPA. Frequency climbing while hold rate falls is a creative running out of road — and by the time the cost per acquisition confirms it, you have paid for the confirmation.
Creative is 49% of what drives the sale, and a quarter of tagging instead of reading is a quarter of spending against the wrong half of it. The ad above loses 38% of viewers at 0:07 — the price overlay landing before the benefit. Nothing in a hook rate or a hold rate says which second to change, so the brief for the next round is written from the same two scalars as the last one. Three more months of that is three more months of reshooting the parts that were working.

# The Change Ledger — every change, undoable — Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/change-ledger

id="main" tabindex="-1">
Change Ledger
The reason you can let it touch the account.
Every change is captured with the exact state it replaced, so putting it back is a restore rather than a reconstruction. That is what makes the difference between a tool you supervise and one you actually use: when a change is genuinely undoable, approving it stops being a small act of courage. The caution you have been carrying was never about the tool — it was about not being able to get back.
Undo is only real if something kept the old value
What it is actually for
The cost of a reversible mistake is an afternoon . The other kind is a quarter.
Ask anyone why they hesitate before letting software change a live account and the answer is never "I want an audit trail". It is that a bad change on a client account is expensive, visible, and hard to walk back — so the safe move is to do nothing, and doing nothing is its own cost.
Without it
Every change is a decision you have to be sure about
So the ones you are unsure about wait for a meeting
Reversing means someone remembering what the number used to be
The account drifts, slowly, in the direction of whatever nobody dared touch
Caution reads as discipline. It is mostly just a cost nobody has priced.
With it
You approve it and watch. The old value is held, so Thursday is a real option.
You test the thing you were unsure about — which is usually the one worth testing.
Reversing is a restore , not four people reconstructing Monday from memory.
You can be wrong on purpose , cheaply, which is the only way anyone learns an account.
The ledger does not make you safer. It makes you faster, because being wrong got cheap.
This is the part that sounds like a compliance feature and is not. A team that can undo anything runs more changes, learns the account faster, and stops routing every ordinary decision through a call. The log is the by-product. The behaviour it unlocks is the point.
Why most undo buttons are not one
A log tells you what happened. It cannot put anything back .
Plenty of tools keep a history, and it reads convincingly right up to the moment you need it. The question is whether the replaced value was captured at the instant of the write — because if it was not, no amount of logging will reconstruct it afterwards.
01
The before-state, captured at the write
Not "budget changed" but the figure it was, stored at the moment it stopped being true. That is the only thing a revert can actually use, and it has to be taken before the change — never inferred later from a report.
02
Reversible or not, said before you approve
Some changes a platform will not take back — a bid strategy with no prior manual bid, a placement that cannot return to its automatic default. You are told which kind you are approving while deciding , not when you try to reverse it and find out.
03
The reversal goes through the same gates
An undo is a write like any other: it re-reads the live account, runs the same guardrails as the forward change, and is logged as its own entry. Reverting a revert works too. Nothing here is a special path that skips the checks.
What an undo sounds like
It is not a button. It is a recommendation you can refuse .
Reversing something is a decision, so it is treated as one. Adgent proposes the inverse change, tells you what it thinks the right call is, and says plainly when the answer depends on something only you know.
Undoing something, six weeks on
This ad was paused back in May and I do not think that was deliberate. Can you put it back?
I can, and here is what I would weigh. It went ACTIVE &rarr; PAUSED on 10 August at 23:47, from chat, approved by you. Reactivating restores it exactly — the other four ads in the set are untouched. If the pause was accidental, this undoes it cleanly. If it was intentional, hold off on approving. I do not know which, and I would rather ask than guess.
It was accidental. Put it back.
Done — PAUSED &rarr; ACTIVE, logged as its own entry. Watch the next few days: if it keeps spending with no clicks, reactivating was the wrong call and it should go back to PAUSED. I can reverse this one too — the revert has a before-state of its own.
The same ad, three entries each reversible
Nothing here is a one-way door.
The part people do not expect
It also catches the changes nobody made.
Ad platforms move things on their own: an automated recommendation applies itself, a bid strategy flips, a budget reallocates under an automation somebody enabled last year. Those are read from the platforms' own change feeds, so drift arrives with a date and a source attached instead of surfacing three weeks later as an unexplained CPA rise. Being honest about the limit: a platform-side change cannot be undone from here — no before-state was captured, because Adgent did not make the write. What it can do is date it, name it, and offer to set the value back as a new change of its own.
Which settles the argument nobody can normally win
"Who changed this, and when?" costs teams more time than almost any other question in a shared ad account, and it is usually unanswerable — so it gets settled by whoever sounds most confident. Here it has a date and a source, including when the answer is the platform itself.
And the before-state is the one thing that cannot be backfilled. Start next quarter and the entries you most want — the bid strategy that flipped at 03:14, the budget that reallocated itself, the setting nobody remembers touching — are already gone, because nothing captured what they replaced at the moment they were replaced. A ledger opened in November cannot restore August. Every month of waiting is a month you can describe but not undo.
Why this matters most on client accounts &rarr; How access is scoped &rarr;
The order it happens in
Read-only &rarr; approve &rarr; reversible .
Three gates, and a change has to pass all of them. None of these is a setting you have to find and switch on.
1 &middot; Read-only by default
A newly connected account has no write access at all. Adgent analyses, ranks and proposes, and cannot touch anything until execution is explicitly enabled for that account.
2 &middot; Nothing applies unapproved
Every proposed change arrives with its before-state, what it is expected to be worth, and whether it can be undone. You approve it from the same chat where you found the problem.
3 &middot; Undo from the same chat
One entry at a time, each rollback logged as its own change. The reversal path is tested against the platforms rather than assumed — reverting is a real operation with its own failure modes, and it is treated like one.
Next
Cheap to undo is only half of it. The other half is not doing it at all.
A reversible change is the floor. The layer above it is the one that declines to make the change in the first place when the account's own numbers say it will not work.
Trust Gate
It refuses unreachable targets before the budget moves.

# Account memory — you explain the account once
URL: https://adgent.app/account-memory

id="main" tabindex="-1">
Account memory
The difference between a tool and someone who knows the account .
Everything that makes your account yours lives in someone&rsquo;s head: the client who will not run video, the market that looks unprofitable and is not, the suggestion you have now rejected four times. None of it is in the ad platforms. It is why a new hire takes a quarter to become useful, and why every generic AI tool still sounds like a stranger on day ninety. Adgent picks these up as you say them — and every verdict after that is written by something that already knows them.
Said once. Applied ever after.
Learned, not configured
There is no setup screen, because nobody fills one in .
Every tool that asks you to declare your rules up front gets a half-finished form and then quietly ignores it. You do not know your exceptions in the abstract — you know them when something violates one. So that is when Adgent picks them up: from what you say in chat, and from what you reject.
It shows you what it learned and asks before keeping it, and you can override any of it. Memory you cannot see is not memory, it is drift.
Adgent · learning
In the background · nothing to manage
You, in chat “Don't scale anything past €500/day without flagging me — we've been burned by fast ramps.”
Adgent will remember this on every campaign
You, in chat “Stop suggesting we merge prospecting and retargeting.”
Noted — suppressed for this account. You can lift it any time
You, in chat “Judge everything against GA4 revenue , not platform ROAS.”
Reports now reconcile to GA4 first
Nothing to fill in up front. Adgent proposes what it heard, you confirm it, and it holds.
Something you only say once
Do not scale anything past €500/day without flagging me. We have been burned by fast ramps.
Noted, and I will hold it. Anything that would take a campaign past €500/day comes to you first, on every account under this brand — Meta and Google.
six weeks later — scale campaign 9, it is working.
It is working, and I would scale it — but that takes it to €640/day, past the limit you set in July. Flagging rather than applying. Say go and it goes.
Held rule six weeks later
The rule outlived the session that set it.
What it actually changes
Memory is what turns an audit into a judgment .
An audit applies general rules to your account. A judgment applies your rules to your account — and that gap is the whole reason a good freelancer is worth more than a good checklist. This is the least visible thing on the site and the one that decides whether people are still using the product in month three.
Week one, any tool
&ldquo;Consider consolidating these campaigns&rdquo; — they are split by client, deliberately
&ldquo;This market is underperforming&rdquo; — it is the one with the highest margin
&ldquo;ROAS is below target&rdquo; — that is not the number you judge on
Every finding needs the same context typed underneath it, again
Technically correct and wrong about your account. On week eight it is saying the same four things.
Week eight, here
The consolidation suggestion is gone — you rejected it in June, and said why.
That market is read on margin , because you told it once that it should be.
Reports reconcile to store revenue first , with platform ROAS beside it as context.
The brief is shorter , because what it already knows is not being re-argued every morning.
Same product, same account. The difference is eight weeks of having been told things.
It stops re-suggesting what you rejected
The fastest way to make someone stop reading a daily brief is to put the same dismissed recommendation in it every morning. Rejecting something twice is information, and it gets treated as information.
It knows which number you judge on
Tell it once that this brand is judged against store revenue rather than platform ROAS, and every report after that reconciles to the store first. Not a per-report setting — a fact about the account.
It carries your limits into execution
"Nothing scales past this without flagging me" is a rule that has to survive to the moment a change is proposed, six weeks later, on a campaign that did not exist when you said it.
Memory is the one thing here that only accrues by starting. A quarter of deferring is a quarter of re-explaining the account every session — the same exceptions retyped, the same rejected suggestion arriving again on Tuesday, the €500/day limit living in someone's head instead of in the thing proposing the change. The context you would have by March is not something you can buy in March. It is only worth what it has been running.
Whose memory it is
Yours, and it follows the brand .
The context belongs to the account, not to one ad platform's view of it. Your rules travel with the brand across every platform you connect, so a decision made about a campaign on one platform is not forgotten when the same question comes up on another.
And it is isolated per company
Each company's data sits in its own database file rather than a shared table with a customer column in it. The separation is structural, so what one account taught Adgent cannot leak into another's verdict.

# What it builds — campaigns, plans, dashboards — Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/built-from-chat

id="main" tabindex="-1">
What it builds
Describe it in a sentence. It gets built .
A campaign, a media plan, a live dashboard, a standing report — four different things, one way of asking for them. Not a template you fill in and not a chart library you assemble. You say what you want; the thing that answers it gets made. And the line that matters runs straight through the middle: two of these only ever read your account, and two of them can change it — so those two are drafted complete, held paused, and wait for you.
One way of asking. Two very different consequences.
Why this exists
The thing you actually want is never the one on the menu .
Every tool ships with a set of views and a set of forms someone else decided you would need. The question in your head at 9am is more specific than any of them — and building it yourself costs the hour you were going to spend on the account.
The hour is the thing to price. One rebuilt-by-hand view a week, at the hour it costs your most expensive person, is most of a working week over a quarter — and that is only the ones that get built. The more expensive ones are the questions nobody asks because the answer would take an afternoon, which is how an account ends up run on the four views that shipped with the tool.
Live dashboards
A view that is still true on Thursday .
Describe the cut you want — the platforms, the window, the breakdown, the metric you judge on — and get the view rather than a form to configure one. What gets built stays wired to the data, so sharing it with a client does not turn it into a screenshot that is wrong by the end of the week.
Asking for a view that does not exist yet
Build me a weekly report by placement, against store revenue, for this client.
Building it now. Placement breakdown across Meta and Google, weekly buckets, reconciled against recorded revenue rather than platform-reported. One thing worth knowing before you send it: Audience Network is 22% of spend and 4% of revenue on this account. It will be the loudest thing on the chart.
Can the client see it live?
Yes — it is a live view, not an export, so it stays current after you share it. Read-only for them. Building a view touches nothing in the account — it only reads.
Built view live
Audience Network: the loudest thing on the chart.
Agents & standing reports
Some things you want once. Some you want every week .
A view you ask for is a one-off. A standing job is the same request, made permanent: the report that rebuilds itself before the Monday call, or an agent watching one specific thing that speaks up only when it moves. You set what it watches and when it should bother you; the rest of the time it stays quiet.
The report that writes itself
The client cut you rebuild every Monday, produced before the call instead of during it — same shape each week, on current data, so the comparison to last week is real rather than reassembled.
An agent per thing you worry about
Set one on the metric you check obsessively — the branded search share, the one campaign that carries the quarter, a placement you do not trust. It watches only that, and stays silent while nothing changes.
Silence is a result
A watcher that reports every day trains you to ignore it. These are built to say nothing until the thing they watch actually moves, which is what makes the message worth opening when it comes.
Media plans
A plan is only worth reading if it shows where the numbers came from .
Every media plan is a stack of forecasts, and almost none of them say what they were forecast from. A cell reading ₺1,400 CPA is either last quarter's campaign or somebody's optimism, and the deck does not tell you which. Adgent drafts the plan as data instead: budget split, flights, line items, and a cost range for each — with the source campaigns and the window printed under every range. Where the account has no history, it writes no number at all and says so.
The plan as a deck
A budget split, agreed in a meeting nobody minuted
A CPA per line, keyed in from memory of last quarter
Every market carries an estimate, including the one you have never run
Assumptions live in the planner's head, and leave when they do
Reviewable only by someone who already knows the account as well as the person who wrote it.
The plan as data
Every cost range names its source campaigns and window. You can open them and check.
The market with no history gets no number. It gets a two-to-four-week test instead, stated as such.
The measurement caveat is in the plan , not discovered in the QBR.
It arrives as a Draft with open questions attached — nothing is applied to any account.
Reviewable by anyone, in the ten minutes before the call.
Asking for the winter plan
Build me a Q4 winter plan for Vestmark. ₺1.85m across the three properties, Nov to end of Jan.
Before I split that, one gap. Norvik and Ashenford both have live search and social history I can price off. Dalmere has none — zero campaigns in this account. I can still give it budget, but I will not attach a cost estimate to it, because there is nothing here to ground one in. Do you want it planned as a test flight, or held back until Norvik proves the season?
Plan it as a test. What does the rest look like?
Draft is up: Google 56 / Meta 44 , six line items, allocated to the exact total. Ranges on four of them with the source campaigns named underneath. One caveat I would not bury: your conversion action carries a value proxy, and a funnel step is dropping before confirmation — so the CPA figures are directional until that is fixed. Nothing is applied. It sits as a Draft until you approve it.
Plan draft Draft &#183; not applied
The gap is stated before the plan, not after it.
01
Every range names its basis
A cost range is written as the campaigns it came from and the window they were read over — not as a figure with a source that lives in someone's head. You can open those campaigns and disagree with the read, which is the only kind of forecast worth reviewing.
02
No history means no number
A market the account has never run in gets budget and a test window, and no estimate at all. The blank is the finding. Filling it with a plausible figure is how a plan starts lying in the first row and keeps the tone for the rest of the page.
03
Approval is per line, not per plan
You can take the two Norvik lines and leave the Dalmere test in draft until the opening date is confirmed. A plan is not a single yes — and producing it touches no campaign, no budget and no setting.
The plan is built from the connected account's own Meta and Google Ads history and nothing else. There is no pooled benchmark under it and no learning carried across from another advertiser — which is also why the empty line stays empty: there is no other account's Dalmere to borrow a number from.
Campaign builds
Built complete. Then held , until you approve it.
Structure, budget, targeting, copy and the creative slots — drafted whole from what you described, prefilled from what this account has actually proven rather than from a template. What you get back is a specification you can read line by line, not a half-configured campaign waiting for twenty more clicks.
Asking for a campaign, and hearing why not yet
Set up a Meta sales campaign for the winter offer. ₺3,500 a week.
I can build it, but check this first. The page and pixel are both connected, so nothing is technically blocking it. But over thirty days that pixel fired 4 purchases — against 16,404 initiate-checkouts and 65,042 custom events. Meta's own guidance puts the floor at 50 events in 7 days. [developers.meta.com] A sales campaign optimising on 4 purchases a month has nothing to learn from. It will spend the ₺3,500 and stay in learning.
So what do I do?
Two options, and I would take the first. Optimise to initiate-checkout instead — 16,404 events is well above the floor — knowing it carries no purchase value, so judge it on bookings, not on the number Meta reports back. Or fix the purchase event first and launch in a fortnight. Say which and I will draft it. It arrives paused either way.
Campaign draft paused &#183; awaiting you
Every choice carries the reason it was made, including the ones it declined.
Prefilled from evidence, not from a template
The bid strategy it proposes is the one proven in this account. The keyword variants are ones that have run. Where it picks something second-best it says why — the ideal option was not available in this ad set.
It blocks in the form, not at the end
A missing creative stops the build where you can still fix it, rather than failing after approval. The same applies to a conversion event that cannot carry value: you are told before, not after.
It arrives paused
Approval creates the campaign in a paused state. Turning it on is a second, separate decision — and like every other write, it lands in the ledger with the state it replaced.
The part that makes it safe
Building something is not the same as doing it.
A drafted plan or campaign is an artifact, not an action. It sits there, fully specified, until you approve it — and when you do, it goes through the same gates as every other change: shown with its before-state, labelled reversible or not, and logged.
And it will tell you when what you asked for will not work
Ask for a campaign built to a target the account has never reached, or a plan for a market with no history behind it, and you get pushback with the account's own numbers attached — before anything is launched. Building on request does not mean building whatever is requested.

The point of building from chat is that you never leave the place you were working. The verdict names the problem, you ask for the thing that shows it, and the fix applies from the same message.

# Paid ads for ecommerce — Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/ecommerce

id="main" tabindex="-1">
For ecommerce & DTC
January's returns rewrite December's ROAS.
19.3% of online sales come back [NRF, Oct 2025]. They come back after the quarter closes — so the number you reported at month-end was provisional and nobody told you. The ad platform never retracts a conversion it already counted, which means your best-performing campaign of the season is graded on revenue that has since walked back out of the building.
The quarter you already reported
Why this one is different
A restated number is worse than a missing one.
Most measurement problems leave a gap you can see. This one leaves a figure that looks complete, gets reported to the board, informs next quarter's budget — and is quietly wrong in one direction only. Returns never make a campaign look worse at the time. They make it look better than it was, for as long as anyone is still paying attention.
What you reported in December
Peak-season revenue, attributed and final
The winning campaign identified, budget planned around it
Everything reconciled and signed off
Correct on the day. Correct in the platform. Not correct.
What January does to it
Roughly a fifth of it comes back — and return rates are not uniform across campaigns, so the ranking changes, not just the totals.
The discount-led campaign returns hardest. The one that looked most efficient is usually the one carrying the highest return rate.
Nothing in the ad account updates. The original figure sits there permanently, informing decisions made all year.
The correction exists in your accounting. It never reaches the system that spent the money.
After the quarter closed
Why does December look worse than it did in December?
Because the returns landed. 19% of the orders attributed to your peak campaigns came back in January, and the ad platforms never retracted the conversions — so their reports still show the original figure. Your two best campaigns swap places once returns are netted out. The discount-led one returned hardest, which is the usual pattern.
Can you catch that earlier next time?
Partly, today: I can flag the campaigns whose order profile looks like the ones that returned last time. Reading refunds directly needs the store connection, which is the next one we are building.
Restated quarter after returns
The discount-led winner returned hardest.
The second thing with no B2B analogue
Ads keep spending after the shelf is empty .
A campaign succeeding hard enough to clear your inventory does not stop. It keeps buying clicks for a product nobody can buy, at the exact moment its performance history says to scale it. There is no version of this problem in lead generation or SaaS — you cannot run out of demos.
Spend is subtracted last
Median DTC gross margin sits near 56.6% , and contribution margin after every deduction lands somewhere between 5% and 35% [analysis of 11 public filers, 2026]. Ad spend comes off beneath cost of goods, processing, shipping and returns — four subtractions the pixel never sees.
Three times return, still losing money
At 3× return on 50% gross margin: a third goes to ads, half to cost of goods, leaving about 17% for shipping, returns, processing and every fixed cost — before roughly a fifth of the orders come back.
Cost peaks exactly when volume does
Peak-season impression costs run far above the annual average, compressed into a handful of days. The most expensive inventory of the year is bought at the moment nobody has time to watch the account.
A quarter is exactly the wrong unit to wait. It is one full return cycle: whatever you set budgets against this quarter gets restated by roughly a fifth next quarter, and the restatement never reaches the account that spent the money. So the discount-led campaign that returns hardest gets funded again, on a ranking that January already corrected. Deciding in three months means deciding with the same overstated number you have now, plus one more season of spend behind it.
Where Adgent stands today
Store reading is the next connection we are building.
Closing this loop properly means reading your store: orders, cost per item, and refunds. That connection is the next one we are building — it is not in the product today — and refund data in particular is what turns "returns restate your quarter" from a true statement about the world into something a tool can act on. Today Adgent reads the ad platforms, GA4, Search Console and Merchant Center. Here is what that already covers.
01
Platform numbers checked against a source it does not control
GA4 sits alongside the ad platforms in every read, so a divergence between what the platform claimed and what the site recorded shows up as a finding rather than as two tabs you compare by hand.
02
Product availability is already in view
Merchant Center feed data — including availability — is read today, which is the first half of catching spend that continues against a product nobody can buy.
03
Creative read scene by scene
Creative is the largest single driver of a campaign's sales, and in peak season it is the lever that moves fastest. Adgent reads the story beat by beat and the exact second viewers leave — on ads already running, with no upload step.
The test you can run yourself, today, without us
Put the ad platforms' reported revenue next to your store's own figure for the same window, then do it again six weeks later. The first comparison tells you how far apart they are. The second tells you how much of what you reported was real — and that second number is the one that should set your budget.
Next
The mechanism underneath, and the lever that moves fastest.
Judging spend against a number the platform cannot see is the general case. Reading the creative is the part of it that already works end to end.
Ground truth
Judged against your real margin, not the number the pixel can see.
Read more
Creative intelligence
Every live ad read scene by scene, with the hold curve.

The same read on every client you run — including the ones nobody opened this week, because attention follows whichever account is currently on fire. It costs the same whether a client spends £10k a month or £1M.
